job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Drafting Review: S. 2817, Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act (Manager's Amendment, Oct. 6)

I worked only from the text you pasted. I haven't checked it against the October 6 amendment as filed, the current U.S. Code, or the 1980 Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act, so verify the citations before publishing. Some items below may be deliberate policy choices rather than errors, so I've framed them as questions for committee staff where that's more accurate.

**Definitions (§2)**

1. **§2(1)(A), volume threshold:** The "10,000 metric tons per year" test applies "by a single vessel," so operators could split recovery across several vessels or stay just under the threshold. The bill also doesn't say how volume is measured (wet or dry weight, nodules recovered or sediment moved).

2. **§2(1)(A), conjunctive test:** Coverage requires all three elements (volume over 10,000 t, depth over 200 m, single vessel). Operations in shallower water, or spread across multiple vessels, fall outside (A), and only (B) could reach them.

3. **§2(1)(A), "commercial" undefined:** The term is defined only by the thresholds, so the bill never says whether sale, offtake, or revenue is relevant. Sub-threshold operations that sell their output may not be "commercial" under the text.

4. **§2(1)(B), "Secretary" and "comparable":** "Secretary" is undefined (§6 specifically says "Secretary of State," which suggests the term means something else elsewhere). "Comparable" risks has no standard, procedure, or notice requirement, which makes a determination easy to challenge as arbitrary and hard for operators to plan around.

5. **§2(2), "U.S. person":** The definition covers citizens and State-organized corporations only, so LLCs, partnerships, and trusts organized under U.S. law are not U.S. persons. "State" is also undefined (does it include D.C. and the territories?).

6. **§2(3), "covered vessel":** "Equipped for" is undefined, and the 5,000-gross-ton threshold leaves smaller vessels outside the registry and reporting regime in §4. The term is also used only in §4, so the prohibition in §3 doesn't depend on it.

**Prohibition (§3)**

7. **§3(a), reach and scope:** "In the United States" is undefined (territorial sea, EEZ, or continental shelf?), and "engage in" doesn't say whether financing, equipment supply, contracting, processing, or importing or selling mined minerals counts. The extraterritorial clause reaches only "U.S. person[s]," so foreign persons and foreign-flagged vessels outside U.S. jurisdiction are not covered.

8. **§3(b), grandfathering:** "Exploration license" is undefined and not tied to an issuing authority. The bill doesn't say whether the exemption covers commercial recovery under an exploration license, whether it can be renewed or transferred, or whether it has any time limit.

9. **§3(c), environmental assessment exemption:** The exemption has no definition, volume cap, permit requirement, reporting duty, or bar on selling the material recovered. An operator could recover commercial volumes and label the activity "assessment." This is the most significant gap in the text.

**Timing (§3, §5, §8)**

10. **Conflicting effective dates:** §8 makes the Act effective 180 days after enactment, but §3(b) keys off enactment, and §5(a) applies penalties to violations "on or after the date of enactment." It's unclear whether conduct during the 180-day window is penalized.

**Registry and reporting (§4)**

11. **§4 has no penalty:** §5 attaches penalties only to violations of §3, so failure to register or file a report carries no stated consequence.

12. **§4(b), report content:** "Describing the recovery activities" is the only content requirement. The bill doesn't specify volumes, coordinates, depths, or discharges, sets no deadline beyond "quarterly," requires no public disclosure, and gives NOAA no duty to review or act on the reports.

**Penalties and enforcement (§5)**

13. **§5(a), "each day":** "Day" is undefined for continuing violations, and the text doesn't say whether each vessel or each ton counts. The $1 million figure is a maximum, with no minimum, gain-based measure, or forfeiture of vessels or ore, so an operator could treat fines as a cost of business. The bill also provides no injunctive relief.

14. **§5, no enforcing agency:** The bill doesn't name an agency or the Justice Department to bring civil actions, and it grants no inspection, subpoena, or investigative authority. It also provides no citizen-suit mechanism. Civil penalties are hard to collect without these tools.

15. **§5(b), criminal provisions:** "Willfully" is undefined, and the bill has no responsible-corporate-officer provision. It doesn't address false certifications under §4(b) directly. General federal false-statement law may apply, but staff should confirm that.

**International agreement (§6)**

16. **§6, "shall seek to negotiate":** This imposes no duty to conclude an agreement, report on progress, or take further action if talks fail. "Equivalent" is undefined, and the section doesn't address potential conflicts with the International Seabed Authority regime under UNCLOS, which the U.S. has not ratified.

**Duration and sunset (§7)**

17. **§7(a), undefined trigger:** "Serious harm" is undefined. The NASEM report has no deadline or scope, and the text doesn't say whether the joint resolution has expedited procedures or how it interacts with presidential signature or veto.

18. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), internal conflict:** §7(a) keeps the prohibition in effect until a joint resolution is enacted, but §7(b) ends the whole Act 10 years after enactment. The prohibition therefore expires at year 10 regardless of any NASEM finding. Because the sunset runs from enactment rather than the §8 effective date, the prohibition would be in force for only about 9.5 years.

19. **§7(b), no savings clause:** The bill doesn't say whether penalties for violations during the operative period survive the sunset, or whether pending enforcement actions continue.

**General drafting and relationship to existing law**

20. **Missing definitions and authority:** The bill doesn't define "recovery," "environmental assessment," or "seabed." It references NOAA in §4 but grants no rulemaking authority, so implementing regulations would have no statutory basis.

21. **No severability or review provisions:** Without a severability clause, a court that strikes §2(1)(B) or §3(c) could leave the scope of the rest uncertain. Vague terms like "comparable" and "serious harm" also invite challenges.

22. **Relationship to existing law:** The bill doesn't say whether it amends, supersedes, or sits alongside the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act of 1980, which NOAA already administers for licensing and permitting. It also doesn't address the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act for activities on the shelf. Staff should confirm whether the §3 exemptions overlap with licenses already issued under those statutes.

**Suggested priorities for markup**

- **Highest:** the §3(c) assessment exemption (item 9), the §7 sunset conflict (item 18), and the enforcement gap (item 14).
- **Next:** the single-vessel and 10,000-ton thresholds (items 1–2), the undefined "Secretary" and "comparable" standard (item 4), and the §4 penalty gap (item 11).
- **Questions for committee staff:** Is the 10-year sunset intended to override §7(a)? Is the §3(c) exemption meant to allow commercial sales? How does the Act interact with existing NOAA licenses under the 1980 Act?
